items.title: Newton's biggest theorem says integration and differentiation are inverses
items.claim: Define F(x) as the area under f from 0 to x. The derivative of F is f. Define G(x) as an antiderivative of f. Then integral from a to b of f dx = G(b) - G(a). Two operations that look unrelated are inverses.

options.text: Integration (continuous summation) and differentiation (instantaneous rate) seem like different operations — but they undo each other. This is one of the most surprising and powerful results in mathematics

items.reveal:
Two parts:

FTC Part I: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F is differentiable on (a, b) and F'(x) = f(x).

FTC Part II: If f is continuous on [a, b] and G is any antiderivative of f (so G'(x) = f(x)), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = G(b) - G(a).

Geometric intuition for Part I: F(x) is area under the curve up to x. As x increases by a small amount dx, the area increases by approximately f(x) * dx — the height at x times the width dx. So dF/dx = f(x).

Why it's surprising:
- Differentiation computes a LOCAL rate at one point.
- Integration sums up TOTAL accumulated value across a range.
- The connection: knowing the total at every point tells you the rate; knowing the rate everywhere tells you the total.

Applications:
- Definite integrals become easy: find an antiderivative, plug in endpoints, subtract.
- Areas, volumes, work, charge, total amounts of accumulated quantities — all computable via antiderivatives.
- Differential equations: solving f' = g is equivalent to finding an antiderivative of g.

Historical: Newton (~1665) and Leibniz (~1675) both discovered it independently. It's the cornerstone of mathematical physics.

Before the FTC, calculating areas under curves (the 'quadrature problem') was a major mathematical challenge — Archimedes computed parabola areas through laborious limit arguments. After the FTC, antiderivatives reduce the problem to algebra.
items.why: Calculus has two halves that look unrelated. The fundamental theorem reveals they are inverses — the same way logarithm and exponential are inverses. This unification is the most powerful idea in elementary mathematics.

items.title: Ice cream sales correlate with drownings — neither causes the other
items.claim: When ice cream sales rise, drowning deaths rise. Strong correlation. Both peak in summer. Neither causes the other — they share a common cause (hot weather drives both ice cream consumption and swimming).
items.prompt: What's wrong with inferring causation from correlation?

options.text: Correlation can arise from: X causes Y; Y causes X; both have a common cause (confounder); selection bias; chance. Without further evidence (experiment or careful causal modelling), we cannot distinguish which
Causation always implies correlation, so causation and correlation are the same

items.reveal_title: Hill criteria, confounders, and the structure of causal inference
items.reveal:
Correlation = statistical association. Causation = mechanistic dependence.

Reasons for correlation without direct causation:
- Common cause (confounder): heat causes both ice cream sales and drownings.
- Reverse causation: rooster crowing 'causes' the sun to rise? Actually opposite.
- Selection bias: hospitalised patients show that brain injury and dietary habits correlate, but only because they were both selected by the hospital criteria.
- Coincidence: with enough variables, spurious correlations are inevitable (https://tylervigen.com/spurious-correlations).

Establishing causation usually requires:
1. Randomised controlled experiment: randomly assign causes, observe effects. Eliminates confounders by design.
2. Natural experiments: variation in cause that's plausibly random (timing of policy changes, weather).
3. Bradford Hill criteria (1965): strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy. Used in epidemiology when RCTs aren't possible.
4. Causal inference frameworks (Pearl's directed acyclic graphs, potential outcomes).

Famous miscalls:
- Hormone replacement therapy and heart disease (observational said 'protective'; RCT said 'harmful').
- Vitamin E and cancer prevention (observational said 'protective'; RCT said 'no effect').
- Coffee and heart disease (many flip-flops).

The replication crisis in psychology and biomedicine partly reflects systematic overinterpretation of correlation as causation.

When RCTs aren't possible (ethics, scale), causal inference is harder but not impossible — but requires careful design and explicit assumption-naming.
items.why: 'Correlation implies causation' is a famous fallacy — but the converse fallacy ('all correlations are meaningless') is also wrong. Understanding the structure of causal evidence is key to scientific literacy.

items.title: 0.9999... equals 1, exactly
items.claim: The decimal expansion 0.999... (infinitely many 9s) does not approach 1 — it IS 1. Two different decimal expansions can represent the same real number.

options.text: They're approximately equal but slightly different
They have zero difference (1 - 0.999... = 0); 0.999... = sum of 9/10 to the n for n from 1 to infinity = 9/10 / (1 - 1/10) = 1 exactly

items.reveal:
Every infinite decimal expansion is, by definition, a convergent series.
0.999... = 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + ...
     = 9/10 * (1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ...)
     = 9/10 * 1/(1 - 1/10)
     = 9/10 * 10/9
     = 1

Another argument: let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x - x = 9.999... - 0.999... so 9x = 9 and x = 1.

Third argument: the difference 1 - 0.999... is less than 10 to the minus n for every n. The only non-negative real with this property is 0. So 1 - 0.999... = 0 and 0.999... = 1.

Decimals are a representation, not an identity. Any real with a terminating decimal also has a 999...-style alternative: 0.5 = 0.4999..., 1 = 0.999..., 0.123 = 0.122999... The two representations are equal.

In educational settings this is one of the most strongly contested results — students often refuse to accept it. The objection is usually based on confusing representations with the numbers themselves.
items.why: Decimals feel like unique addresses for numbers. They are not — every terminating decimal has a recurring-9 twin, and equality of the two is logically forced.
